documents.abstract: Abstract Study Design Cross-sectional natural language processing (NLP) study of publicly available Reddit data. Objectives To map the thematic structure and affective tone of neuropathic pain discourse among Reddit users self-identifying with spinal cord injury (SCI) or clinically overlapping cord and cauda pathology, and to surface candidate hypotheses for triangulation with patient-reported and clinical data. Setting Public Reddit communities. Methods Searches across ten subreddits using twenty query strings yielded 1489 candidate posts. A two-tier keyword filter (SCI-spectrum population term plus a pain or treatment term) retained 517 unique documents from six communities. Documents were embedded with a sentence-transformer model, reduced with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and clustered using KMeans (K = 10) within a BERTopic representation pipeline, with the cluster count and cluster labels informed by a lexically derived seed-topic list. Cluster stability and sensitivity to the choice of K were assessed. Themes were characterised by class-term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) keywords and provisional large language model labelling. Sentiment was assigned using a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned on social media text; because the classifier was not calibrated in this clinical domain, sentiment proportions are reported as directional, ordinal signals rather than calibrated estimates. Engagement was operationalised as median upvote score and comment count per theme. Results The corpus was dominated by r/spinalcordinjuries (41%) and r/ChronicPain (23%). Overall sentiment was negative in 56.1% of posts (uncalibrated). Ten interpretable themes were identified within this two-community corpus. The highest negative-sentiment shares were in Treatment-Refractory Pain and Psychological Burden, Opioid and Polypharmacy Management Challenges, and Severe Spasticity Progression; the lowest were in Spinal Cord Stimulation Devices and Advanced Neuromodulation. Engagement was highest for crisis narratives (median upvote score 13) and opioid-management discourse (median 22 comments). Conclusions Within the sampled Reddit communities, discourse on neuropathic pain in SCI and overlapping cord/cauda pathology is dominated by negative affect, treatment refractoriness, and psychosocial burden, while emerging neuromodulation themes attract comparatively less negative sentiment. Findings are signal-generating, require triangulation with clinical data, and should not be read as representative of the broader SCI population. Sponsorship None.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful instrument to solve complex problems related to sustainable water resource management because it allows creating advanced, data-driven modelling, prediction, and optimization of water systems. Although the studies in this sphere have increased quickly, the global scientific tendencies have not been thoroughly examined. This research paper presents a bibliometric review of the literature about AI applications in green water management that was published from 2015 to 2025. The Scopus database was searched with a structured search strategy on bibliographic data, and 3,280 peer-reviewed articles were analyzed. VOSviewer was used to perform bibliometric mapping and network visualization to investigate the trends in publications, most active journals, most impactful authors, contributions of institutions, country-level partnerships, and research clusters. The findings indicate that the publishing activity has grown tremendously in the last ten years, which suggests that there is a growing interest in AI-based solutions to water quality monitoring, hydrological prediction, optimization of wastewater treatment, and smart water management system. China, the United States and India became the most productive nations with the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Beijing normal university as some of the top contributing institutions. The analysis of the key words co-occurrence (dominant research themes) was based on machine learning, water-quality prediction, hydrological modelling, remote sensing, and decision-support systems. The co-citation analysis has shown the core studies in machine learning algorithms, including random forests, neural networks, and boosting algorithms, which underpin the present studies in this field. Overall, the results depict the growing role of AI technologies to enhance the effectiveness of water resources management and wastewater treatment. This research offers a clear insight into the intellectual framework and the future research perspective of AI-based environmentally sustainable water management which can be of great value to researchers, policymakers, and practitioners who would wish to come up with innovative and data-based water management solutions.

Abstract The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality, and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist most of the time. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108–1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure–property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In a broader context, we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

Background.Cancer during pregnancy poses a dual clinical challenge: maternal disease must be controlled without compromising fetal safety, yet prediction of outcomes is hampered by fragmented multimodal data and the absence of models that adapt as pregnancy advances.We developed a maternal-fetal oncology framework combining a multimodal foundation model with continuously updated patient-specific digital twins to support cancer prediction, risk stratification, treatment optimization, and joint maternal-fetal outcome forecasting. Methods.A retrospective cohort of 350 pregnant women diagnosed with cancer was assembled from four tertiary centers, spanning breast, cervical, ovarian, thyroid, melanoma, lymphoma, and leukemia.The framework (MFO-FM) integrates clinical, imaging, genomic, and laboratory encoders through a maternal-fetal fusion module, while a digital twin ecosystem assimilates longitudinal maternal physiology, fetal physiology, cancer progression, and treatment response.Performance was benchmarked against logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and a deep neural network using five-fold cross-validation and an external test set.Results.MFO-FM achieved an accuracy of 0.927, F1-score of 0.916, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.958, exceeding XGBoost (AUC 0.911) and the deep neural network (AUC 0.928).Favorable maternal outcomes occurred in 262 of 350 women (74.9%) and healthy neonatal outcomes in 214 of 350 (61.1%), with preterm birth in 97 (27.7%).Cancer stage, gestational age at diagnosis, and chemotherapy timing were the dominant predictors.The digital twin reproduced observed trajectories with a concordance index of 0.85.Conclusions.An adaptive foundation model coupled with digital twin ecosystems delivered accurate, interpretable, trimester-aware predictions across the maternal-fetal oncology continuum.Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical adoption.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

Generative AI (GenAI) is embedded in design education, yet little is known about how different tools reshape metacognition and the pathways linking ideas to outcomes. We compare three conditions, ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and a no-AI control, in a virtual reality cultural heritage serious game task with 51 novice designers. Think-aloud, screen recordings, sketches, and AI logs were coded into network-based cognitive maps and event-anchored indicators around metacognitive nodes. Analyses combine expert ratings of design outcomes with thinking pathway profiles and window diversity after metacognitive events. Both GenAI groups show higher mean design-quality ratings than the control, but in complementary ways. DeepSeek broadens early ideation and shows higher novelty ratings, while ChatGPT strengthens metacognitive regulation and structured convergence, aligning with higher systematicity and interactivity. The findings introduce process-sensitive indicators and phase-aware guidance for configuring exploration-oriented and regulation-oriented assistance in human and AI co-creation.

As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

Large language models for code have achieved strong performance across diverse software analytics tasks, yet their real-world adoption remains limited by high computational demands, slow inference speeds, significant energy consumption, and environmental impact. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical solution by transferring knowledge from a large model (teacher) to a smaller and more efficient model (student). Despite its effectiveness, recent studies show that models distilled from a single teacher often exhibit degraded adversarial robustness, even when robustness-aware distillation techniques are employed. These observations suggest a fundamental limitation of single-teacher distillation in simultaneously transferring high-quality and robust knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we propose Mixture of Experts Knowledge Distillation (MoEKD), a KD framework that leverages a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to enable more effective and robust knowledge transfer from multiple specialized experts into a compact model. MoEKD decomposes the distillation process into expert and router training, aggregation of expert knowledge through a learned routing mechanism, and distillation from the aggregated knowledge. We evaluate MoEKD on the vulnerability detection task using CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT models. Experimental results show that MoEKD not only improves adversarial robustness by up to 35.8%, but also enhances predictive performance by up to 13%, compared to state-of-the-art KD baselines, including Compressor and AVATAR. Moreover, MoEKD-based students exhibit greater behavioral fidelity to their teachers, indicating better preservation of the teacher's predictive behavior after distillation. Deployment efficiency and environmental sustainability evaluations further show that MoEKD-based students maintain deployment costs comparable to their single-teacher counterparts, with slightly lower inference latency, energy consumption, and carbon emissions observed in most CPU and GPU settings. Our ablation analyses show that MoEKD retains its performance and robustness advantages under more aggressive student compression, while lightweight heterogeneous experts substantially reduce offline training costs and largely preserve its performance gains, but exhibit reduced adversarial robustness. The router analysis further shows that top-2 expert selection mitigates top-1 routing errors, while routing quality influences both the aggregated knowledge and the resulting student performance. Overall, these findings highlight the effectiveness of multi-expert knowledge aggregation in addressing key limitations of existing single-teacher KD approaches.

Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

As large language models increasingly match human performance on moral-judgment tasks, two bodies of literature have developed in parallel. Empirical moral psychology treats moral judgment as an output and benchmarks artificial systems against human responses. The philosophy of artificial moral agency denies agency to such systems mainly on the ground of sentience, an empirically inaccessible criterion that has left the debate stalled. This paper argues that human–AI convergence in moral judgment conceals a categorical asymmetry that neither literature has theorized. Drawing on Spinoza’s conatus and Damasio’s account of homeostasis and affect, it argues that moral agency presupposes affective-homeostatic self-maintenance as its constitutive ground: the organization from which valuation first arises. This condition is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim is constitutive rather than normative, so it does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” Sentience is repositioned as the experiential manifestation of this organization rather than the explanatory terminus. Contemporary AI systems, including those trained with human feedback, are therefore moral judges without moral agency. The paper closes with a behavioral research program, including concrete experimental designs, on the conditions under which people attribute moral agency to human and artificial agents.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: The first essay is a meta-analysis that provides the first systematic examination of how the AI–human gap in customer responses varies across customer journey stages, and how anthropomorphic design factors moderate this gap at each stage. Analyzing 1,425 effect sizes drawn from 401 studies reported in 129 publications, I document a small but robust baseline disadvantage for AI agents relative to human agents (r̄ = −.140). The gap is largest in pre-purchase stage, where inflated performance expectations amplify disappointment when shortfalls occur, and smallest in post-purchase stage, where lower expectations for AI emotional capability mean that adequate performance can exceed consumer baselines. To explain these patterns, I introduce experience-dimension primacy, a mechanism specifying that cognitive, affective, and social customer experience dimensions shift in relative salience across journey stages, systematically altering how AI agents are evaluated at each point in the journey. Identity cues, form cues, and interaction cues produce pronounced stage-contingent reversals: the same design choice that reduces the AI–human gap at one stage can widen it at another. Taken together, these findings challenge uniform AI deployment strategies and provide actionable guidance for aligning agent design with the dominant experiential dimension at each stage of the customer journey. The second essay examines AI social role design through the lens of brand biography. Firms increasingly deploy AI agents as the primary consumer interface, yet whether their appropriate social role depends on the brand's narrative identity remains unknown. Drawing on the congruity schema, this research explores whether partner-framed AI is congruent with underdog brands and servant-framed AI with top dog brands, advancing perceived congruence as the mechanism and examining perceived power imbalance as an initially proposed mediator, with self-brand connection as a moderator. In Study 1, partner-framed AI produced more favorable responses under both brand biographies, and perceived power imbalance did not mediate. In Study 2, the predicted congruency pattern emerged only among consumers with low self-brand connection, on social experience, satisfaction, perceived congruence, and customer experience, operating through perceived congruence. Therefore, Brand-AI congruency is conditional, holding for consumers without an established brand relationship.

Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}

BART (Bay Area Rapid Transit) serves commuters, students, and visitors in the Bay Area. However, ridership has declined due to rising crimes, drug use, sexual assaults, and homelessness. These challenges disproportionately impact women and minorities, many of whom report discomfort, distrust in the system, and negative safety perceptions (Alliance for Girls Youth, 2024). The goal is to examine how safety perception influences BART riders’ experiences and decision making through the lenses of Human Factors and Industrial Engineering. We conducted a mixed-method research to understand perceived risk, environmental awareness, and support riders’ needs when commuting. Participants, particularly women, had reported feeling unsafe at night, traveling in groups, strategically choosing seatings, and staying vigilant in fear of being harmed. Riders also expressed interest in a verified “buddy feature,” safety alerts, and reporting incidents. Overall, this highlights opportunities to improve safety, build trust, and improve the commuting experience for BART.

This study examined how project managers navigate wicked problem dynamics in project environments with ambiguous problem definitions, contested stakeholder interests, evolving constraints, and no definitive solutions. Drawing on eight nested discussion sessions comprising 24 small-group conversations with 168 experienced project professionals across diverse industries, supplemented by 12 follow-up interviews, the study used a theory-informed abductive qualitative design. Adaptive leadership and wicked problem concepts informed the discussion prompts, whereas initial coding remained open to participants’ accounts rather than applying a predetermined adaptive-leadership coding framework. We then iteratively interpreted emergent patterns using wicked problems theory, adaptive leadership, and sensemaking as sensitizing theoretical lenses. The analysis identified five recurring adaptive practices: diagnostic framing, collaborative sensemaking, situational awareness, emotional regulation, and transparent communication. These practices illuminate how project managers develop workable problem definitions, engage competing perspectives, and coordinate action when technical expertise and established plans are insufficient. The study provides an empirically grounded account of leadership practice in temporary organizations and identifies practice-oriented implications for responding to wicked problem dynamics within time-bounded project settings.

Near-real-time wildfire monitoring is essential for situational awareness and emergency response. The Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observes at 2 km every 5 min, whereas the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observes at 375 m twice daily, leaving neither sensor able to track rapidly evolving fires in fine spatial detail. This study introduces a two-step deep learning approach that statistically infers VIIRS-like sub-pixel fire segmentation and brightness temperature (BT) from GOES imagery. The dataset comprises 257 U.S. wildfires within preselected regions of interest, pairing multi-spectral GOES imagery with VIIRS-derived references in four classes (Non-Fire, Small, Medium, and Large) defined by the number of fire pixels. Against an autoencoder-based baseline, the proposed method raises average precision from 0.105 to 0.368 and reduces the fire region BT root mean square error by 72.1% from 81.33 K to 22.69 K. Omission error rates fall from 9.41% to 1.96% for Medium fires and remain at zero for Large fires, whereas Small fires, 37% of the test set, remain at 39.91%. The false positive rate on Non-Fire images falls from 66.86% to 8.48%, near the operational GOES product’s 6.36% with lower omission (31.40% versus 40.35%). Inference completes within 5 min of observation for a monitored region.

Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long- horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves 23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca, yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

Terrestrial network (TN) failures during disasters can overload surviving base stations (BSs) and disrupt emergency services. A non-terrestrial network (NTN) provides fallback, but its feeder link can become a bottleneck as users migrate. This paper studies post-disaster network resilience through service-priority-aware orchestration of constrained NTN feeder capacity in a post-failure snapshot. A lightweight Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) tunes feeder, offload, and user-ranking parameters offline, not as an online artificial intelligence (AI) controller. A Python system-level simulator sweeps operating regions under abstract TN-NTN link and queueing models. Gains depend on failure severity. At a 180-Mbps feeder under total TN outage, the proposed policy increases the absolute emergency-weighted continuity metric Cemg from 0.399 to 0.666 relative to the matched rule baseline with uniform feeder scaling (paired gain: 0.267; 95% bootstrap CI: [0.264, 0.271]); mild damage can reduce aggregate continuity. Offline CEM feeder-weight tuning further improves severe-failure continuity over fixed service priorities, whereas tuned offload and user ranking provide no detectable incremental gain.

Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs) aim to capture clinically useful information beyond sleep staging, yet are rarely compared with sleep-staging encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage. Using a common whole-night, missingness-aware state-space downstream modeling framework, we compared frozen representations from prominent large-scale, multi-cohort sleep-stage-supervised encoders and self-supervised PSG FMs for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups in 7,906 PSGs from an unseen registry. Although PSG FMs outperformed an EEG-only, single-cohort supervised baseline, this ordering reversed when supervised pretraining approached comparable scale and modality coverage. Transfer learning from neural sleep scorers achieved higher overall performance while exhibiting greater downstream data efficiency. These findings underscore the need for scale- and modality-matched pretrained supervised baselines when assessing PSG FMs' downstream potential.

Calibration has been extensively studied for classifiers, but remains largely unexplored for crowdsourcing aggregation methods, which are increasingly used for making probabilistic decisions. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical and empirical study of calibration in label aggregation. To our great surprise, we find that widely used aggregation methods can be severely miscalibrated, and in opposite directions: Majority Vote is underconfident while model-based aggregators are overconfident. We prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its data-generating model. We also show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions, which helps explain why Majority Vote is generally miscalibrated in realistic crowds. Empirically, we study calibration across $39$ human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds. In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $ϕ$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $ϕ$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.

Latte art is a complex task requiring dexterity and precision, making it a challenging and commercially relevant task. A one-shot learning system is employed in which a single barista demonstration is segmented into five functionally distinct phases, each encoded as an independent Cartesian Dynamic Movement Primitive (CDMP) with its own parameters. Against a single-CDMP baseline, per-phase encoding reduces transition endpoint error by 3.2-4.5 times and art-stroke shape error by 2.7 times, reproducing jug tilt to below 1 degree RMS in the pouring phases. The learnt pour scales from a 280mL to a 400mL cup through a single spatial offset and a scaled recipe, with no re-demonstration. The phase-based CDMP approach generalises beyond latte art to any demonstration task whose phases have distinct spatial or temporal requirements whilst demonstrating the ability to adapt reproductions to suit different task requirements.

Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: In 1985, Richard Stallman introduced copyleft, a licensing principle that allows source code to be used, modified, and redistributed provided that the same freedoms are preserved in derivative works (Stallman, 1985). Although developed for software, copyleft offers a useful analogy for ecological research, where data, metadata, and analytical code should be accessible and reusable under clear licenses. Similarly, our ability to understand and address ecological challenges such as biodiversity loss, species range shifts, land degradation, and climate change depends on ecological knowledge being open where ethically appropriate and otherwise responsibly accessible. Such knowledge should also be managed according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and established domain standards such as Darwin Core and Ecological Metadata Language (Wieczorek et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2016). Despite substantial progress in open science (Dwivedi et al. 2022), many key ecological datasets (e.g., national ecological inventories, biodiversity records, and high-spatial- and temporal-resolution remote-sensing data) remain proprietary or available only with restricted access (e.g., requiring formal approval). These gaps are substantial: Large-scale analyses of hundreds of millions of ecological records reveal persistent taxonomic, geographic, and temporal biases (Meyer et al. 2015, Daru and Rodriguez, 2023). Much of the scientific literature also remains behind paywalls, while open-access publication fees can create barriers for researchers with limited funding (Rocchini and Neteler 2012). This paradox, that is, publicly funded knowledge becoming inaccessible to the public, constrains who can participate in ecological research and which ecosystems, regions, and perspectives are ultimately represented. AI does not create this problem but can amplify it by embedding data biases in models reused at scale, while closed training data limit independent scrutiny (Koch et al. 2022). AI for ecology encompasses task-specific machine-learning and computer-vision models, as well as foundation models, including large language models (LLMs). These systems differ in scale, purpose, and accessibility, but all depend on the quality, documentation, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate them. By integrating diverse data sources, AI can transform ecological research. However, when data, code, or model-development processes cannot be independently inspected, existing knowledge gaps and biases may be transferred into ecological inference. Appropriately open, reliable, and interoperable ecological data, together with transparent and auditable AI infrastructures, are therefore essential for robust, equitable, and epistemically sound ecological research. The expansion of AI in ecological research intensifies the need for transparent and well-documented knowledge. Bias is not unique to AI: statistical, mechanistic, and machine-learning models can all inherit limitations from their data and assumptions. AI can increase the scale, opacity, and reach of these effects (Han et al. 2023). Currently, many applications in ecology use task-specific AI models trained for bounded prediction or classification problems (Pichler and Hartig 2023). These models are often trained on specialized aggregated ecological repositories (e.g., biodiversity data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility [GBIF]), climatic variables (e.g., from WorldClim and ERA5), or land-use and land cover change mapping (e.g., from satellite imagery). In contrast, the rise of foundation models, including LLMs used for the automated synthesis of scientific literature, code generation, data processing and analysis, requires massive cross-domain training sets that are difficult to build from scratch. Consequently, models trained on skewed, geographically biased, or inaccessible datasets can systematically misrepresent under-sampled regions and reflect long-standing inequities in ecological knowledge. When training datasets are inaccessible, their composition is also difficult to inspect, making gaps in the representation of regions, languages, taxa, or perspectives harder to detect and evaluate. Thus, LLMs are not necessarily more biased than task-specific AI models, but their biases can be harder to trace and hence propagate across a wider range of users, tasks, and applications. In ecology, both task-specific and generic models inherit the limitations of the data used to train them. For example, species-recognition models inherit taxonomic imbalances in training images (Koch et al. 2022), whereas LLMs can process ecological information rapidly but may perform poorly on specific tasks. Gougherty and Clipp (2024) found that LLMs often struggled to extract pathogen-incidence values and sometimes inferred that all individuals were affected when no incidence value was reported. Similarly, Dorm et al. (2026) showed that LLMs performed poorly in generating species range maps and offered only limited improvement over random guessing in threat classification. Comparable effects have been observed in other AI domains, where imbalances in training data have produced systematically poorer model performance for underrepresented groups (Birhane, 2022). Together, these examples illustrate how unbalanced training data can transfer existing knowledge gaps into model outputs, highlighting the importance of identifying, documenting, and reducing such biases before models are applied beyond their validated domain. AI models can furthermore introduce subtler epistemic risks (Loru et al. 2025), including the confident fabrication of ecological information, the misrepresentation of species-trait responses to environmental gradients, and the generation of unsupported ecological interactions or spatial patterns. In ecological applications, documented limitations already include errors in quantitative information extraction and uneven performance across tasks (Gougherty and Clipp, 2024, Dorm et al. 2026). For these reasons, responsible openness and transparent governance of ecological data and metadata are vital, because the reliability of specialized models and large-scale synthesis depends on whether foundational ecological resources can be appropriately accessed, documented, and independently evaluated. Reproducible evaluation therefore requires practical commitments. Ecological AI studies should provide standardized documentation describing where their training data came from, which taxa, regions, and environmental conditions they cover, how the model is intended to be used, and its known limitations. Established tools such as datasheets for datasets and model cards can support this documentation (Gebru et al. 2021). Models should also be evaluated across taxa, regions, languages, and environmental conditions, and data, code, prompts, model weights, and independent evaluation sets should be released where ethically, legally, and technically possible (Maasri et al. 2022, Smith et al. 2024). In order to improve data exchange and utilization, general principles and standards for the creation, verification, and sharing of data should be established while respecting the owners and creators of specific databases. Any restrictions and access procedures should also be documented. Public initiatives such as the Minerva LLM (Orlando et al. 2024) illustrate the value of transparent, language-specific model development, but openness alone does not ensure ecological or cultural validity across regions. AI also changes the politics of openness by creating a risk that openly shared data and open-source code are incorporated into proprietary models without reciprocal access, attribution, credit, or participation for the researchers, developers, and communities who produced them. In public and public/private programs such as GenAI4EU (2025), adequate funding should mean sustained support for data curation, digitization of legacy records, targeted collection in documented gaps, local skills and infrastructure, and independent auditing, not only model development. Funders, publishers, scientific societies, and research institutions should recognize data curation as a research output and require transparent documentation and evaluation. Collaboration should connect local communities and data holders to national infrastructures, international repositories, and standards bodies. Identifying and reducing bias in AI development, enabling robust validation, and sustaining open infrastructures all depend fundamentally on the availability of high-quality, representative, and well-documented ecological data. Where data are scarce, uneven, or unreliable, transparency becomes especially important for identifying gaps and assessing their consequences (Titley et al. 2017). Open data and governance policies must therefore be accompanied by dedicated funding for targeted data collection, the digitization of legacy records, curation, metadata preparation, quality control, local computational infrastructure, training, and equitable collaboration, particularly in under-sampled regions. Such investments are necessary to prevent openness from disproportionately benefiting institutions that already possess the resources needed to exploit shared datasets. Openness should not, however, imply unrestricted public release. Precise locations of threatened species, Indigenous and local knowledge, and data governed by consent or legal agreements may require spatial generalization, controlled access, embargoes, or community authority (Tulloch et al. 2018). Data should instead be as open as possible and as protected as necessary, combining FAIR data stewardship with the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) where Indigenous or community-governed data are involved. International coordination among funders, ecological societies, repositories, publishers, data providers, and model developers is also needed to establish interoperable standards for data collection, annotation, documentation, sharing, and controlled access. Differences in the quality, resolution, and accessibility of ecological datasets should be explicitly documented and considered during model development and evaluation rather than remaining hidden (Dwivedi et al. 2022). Without shared standards and a commitment to responsible openness, ecological AI risks becoming fragmented, opaque, and shaped primarily by actors with the greatest computational and data resources. The practical priorities that we highlight are the following. Ecologists, AI researchers, funders, journals, repositories, and ecological societies should: audit geographic, taxonomic, temporal, and, where relevant, linguistic gaps in AI training and evaluation data, and quantify their effects on model performance; fund targeted data collection and the digitization of legacy records where these gaps have meaningful consequences; require machine-readable metadata and licenses, provenance records, uncertainty documentation, datasheets for datasets, and model cards; maintain independent benchmark datasets stratified across regions, taxa, sensors, and environmental conditions; and ensure that data-producing communities have access to computational infrastructure, training, credit, and decision-making roles rather than being treated solely as data providers (Wilkinson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2024). Ecological research stands at a decisive crossroad: As AI reshapes how we observe and interpret the natural world, the openness and responsible governance of our data, models, and publications will determine whether this transformation is equitable and scientifically robust. Unrepresentative datasets, or data and models that cannot be independently evaluated, risk narrowing ecological insight, reinforcing global disparities, and introducing epistemic distortions that degrade our collective understanding of ecological systems. A well-governed, participatory, and inclusive ecological knowledge system, open where possible and protected where necessary, supported by public LLM research, auditable domain-specific models, and genuinely accessible publishing practices, is crucial to ensure that AI becomes a tool for discovery and justice rather than distortion. Just as copyleft preserved the freedoms to use, modify, and share software, responsible openness can free environmental science from informational silos while respecting legitimate restrictions. In the age of AI, openness is not only a technical requirement but an ethical obligation: Shared and responsibly governed knowledge is the foundation of collective solutions. There are no new data associated with this article. The authors declare no competing interests.

Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

documents.abstract: Abstract The automotive industry’s operations face a critical dilemma: achieving high productivity while maintaining adequate ergonomic standards. High-volume production amplifies this condition, because the frequency of task execution keeps ergonomic risk ever-present. This work presents a real case from an automotive body parts assembly line. The objectives are to minimize the maximum individual ergonomic risk throughout job-rotation periods along a daily journey, and to optimize productivity by determining the optimal worker-to-workstation assignments. The Occupational Repetitive Action (OCRA) index is used to assess the risk of upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders. To solve this bi-objective problem, two algorithms are proposed: an $$\varepsilon $$ ε -constraint approach and a Tchebychev method. Both are grounded in a novel Integer Linear Programming (ILP) model tailored to integrate ergonomic and productivity considerations. The algorithms generated a complete Pareto front of 16 efficient solutions within a reasonable computational time. Managerial insights are derived, highlighting the inherent trade-off between the makespan and ergonomic risk, providing valuable guidelines for balancing worker well-being and productivity in assembly-line operations.

This study analyzes the relationship between digitalization, structural transformation, and carbon emission intensity in six ASEAN countries, namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The study uses annual panel data for the period 2004–2024, with the main estimation period covering 2010–2024. Carbon emission intensity is used as the dependent variable, while the number of internet users, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, international trade, and services sector value added are used as independent variables. All variables are transformed into natural logarithms so that the coefficients can be interpreted as elasticities. Estimation is conducted using the Fixed Effects Model with period fixed effects and Panel EGLS with period weights following model selection tests. The results show that digitalization, proxied by the number of internet users, has a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with carbon emission intensity. In contrast, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, and international trade have positive and significant relationships. Services sector value added has a negative and significant relationship with carbon emission intensity. These findings indicate that structural transformation toward the services sector is associated with lower emission intensity, while industrial expansion, urbanization, economic growth, and trade are associated with increased carbon emission intensity in the countries examined.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article examines the linguodidactic foundations for forming and developing the AI competence of both educators and students within the context of the effective use of artificial intelligence technologies in language education. Amidst digital transformation, artificial intelligence-specifically generative language models, chatbots, speech recognition systems, automated assessment tools, and adaptive learning platforms-is becoming a new component of the foreign language teaching and learning process. The article defines an educator's AI competence as a composite of technological knowledge, methodological-pedagogical competence, critical evaluation skills, awareness of ethics and digital security, and the ability to integrate AI tools into language education.

Kelawi Tourism Village, South Lampung, has strong community-based tourism potential, but the Minang Rua Bahari Tourism Awareness Group (Pokdarwis) faces communication barriers when serving international visitors. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to strengthen Pokdarwis capacity through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted voice service as a communication support tool. The program was conducted from 12 to 14 June 2026 and involved 15 Pokdarwis members. Activities included problem identification, local knowledge development and validation, QR-based service implementation, training, mentoring, and evaluation at four service points: visitor reception, turtle conservation, Green Canyon, and homestay and culinary services. Results showed an increase in partner capacity from 58.2% in the pre-test to 91.8% in the post-test, representing a 33.6 percentage-point improvement. Participant satisfaction reached 92%, while partner and visitor achievement rates reached 95.2% and 94.5%, respectively. The program demonstrates that AI can support communication, conservation, safety, and the delivery of local cultural and culinary information without replacing the role of Pokdarwis.

This study aimed to examine the effect of intrinsic motivation on students' active participation in extracurricular activities at SMK Negeri 7 Makassar. A quantitative approach with a causal associative research design was employed. The population consisted of 256 students participating in extracurricular activities, with a sample of 155 students selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression analysis. The findings showed that both intrinsic motivation and students' active participation were categorized as high. The regression analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation had a positive and significant effect on students' active participation, with a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the coefficient of determination (R² = 0.247) indicated that intrinsic motivation contributed 24.7% to students' active participation, while the remaining 75.3% was influenced by other factors beyond the scope of this study. These findings indicate that higher levels of intrinsic motivation are associated with higher levels of students' active participation in extracurricular activities.

Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) is an essential component of practical learning in the Electric Power Network Engineering (TJTL) program because students are exposed to electrical and workshop hazards. This study aimed to develop an OHS educational video and determine its feasibility, student response, and the increase in students’ understanding after use. The study employed Research and Development (R&D) with the 4-D model consisting of Define, Design, Develop, and Disseminate. Product validation involved three expert validators consisting of one media expert and two OHS experts, while user feasibility was assessed by three teacher practitioners. Student response involved 29 students, and the increase in understanding was examined using a one-group pretest-posttest design and N-Gain analysis. The mean feasibility score was 4.50 from the expert-media assessment and 4.82 from the practitioner assessment, both in the “very good” category. Student response reached a mean score of 4.78, also in the “very good” category. The mean N-Gain was 0.86, classified as high, indicating a substantial increase in test scores after the video was used. The findings support the use of the video as a contextual learning aid for OHS preparation before TJTL practical activities. However, the effectiveness evidence is limited because the study used one group without a comparison group and measured cognitive understanding rather than actual safety behavior.

The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

Performance uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable validation and eventual clinical translation of medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI). Confidence intervals (CIs) play a central role in this process by indicating how precise a reported performance estimate is. Yet, due to the limited amount of work examining CI behavior in medical imaging, the community remains largely unaware of how many diverse CI methods exist and how they behave in specific settings. The purpose of this study is to close this gap. To this end, we conducted a large-scale empirical analysis across a total of 24 segmentation and classification tasks, using 19 trained models per task group, a broad spectrum of commonly used performance metrics, multiple aggregation strategies, and several widely adopted CI methods. Reliability (coverage) and precision (width) of each CI method were estimated across all settings to characterize their dependence on study characteristics. Our analysis revealed five principal findings: (1) the sample size required for reliable CIs varies from a few dozens to several thousands of cases depending on study parameters; (2) CI behavior is strongly affected by the choice of performance metric; (3) aggregation strategy substantially influences the reliability of CIs, e.g. they require more observations for macro than for micro; (4) the machine learning problem (segmentation versus classification) modulates these effects; (5) different CI methods are not equally reliable and precise depending on the use case. Finally, we derived practical implications of this study in the form of a decision tree which shall prove useful to the community. This paves the way for future consensus guidelines on reporting performance uncertainty.

documents.abstract: Abstract Agentic AI systems commonly combine a general-purpose AI model with prompts, tools, orchestration and an external memory layer. The model need not be fine-tuned: records retrieved from persistent memory are normally inserted into the model’s inference-time context and can thereby influence later outputs and actions without changing model weights. This article asks how far the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) already govern the risks that follow. It reframes persistent memory as a system feature that can mediate or amplify misalignment and emergent behaviour, rather than as training data or a new category in the AI Act’s use-case-based taxonomy. Article 15 provides a clear legal anchor for robustness and cybersecurity, while Articles 9–14, 25, 72 and 73 extend coverage across risk management, data governance, logging, oversight, value-chain responsibility and post-market monitoring. For organisations within NIS2’s scope, Articles 20, 21 and 23 add entity-level governance, all-hazards cybersecurity, supply-chain controls and incident reporting. The remaining problem is therefore not a wholesale absence of law. It is whether these overlapping duties are sufficiently operationalised for memory-mediated failures such as poisoned retrieval, scope leakage, stale reliance, revocation failure and loss of provenance. The article proposes proportionate implementation through existing guidance, standards, documentation and monitoring mechanisms, without creating a new statutory risk tier or a memory-specific regulatory regime.

documents.abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.

Background and objective: Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and medical research represents significant potential; however, it also introduces practical and ethical challenges. This study analyzes physicians' perceptions of AI implementation in clinical and academic settings, exploring their awareness, perceptions, barriers, concerns, and insights into ethical and regulatory considerations. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used. The quantitative component involved standardized surveys completed by 390 physicians (241 clinical, 149 academic) in Erbil City from November 2024 to June 2025. Participants were selected using systematic sampling, and surveys were self-administered. The qualitative component included two focus group discussions, involving 6 clinical physicians and 8 academic physicians, to explore in-depth perceptions and concerns regarding AI in healthcare and research. Results: Of 390 physicians, the majority of participants were male (69.2%). Mean age was 46.7±7 years. Familiarity with AI was higher among younger, male, and academic physicians, with age showing a negative association (p <0.001). Clinical physicians reported more concerns regarding privacy in healthcare (p=0.003) and research (p=0.041), as well as algorithmic bias (p=0.030). Despite these concerns, most physicians valued AI in healthcare and academic research and demonstrated strong interest in training and collaboration. Qualitative findings showed optimism and frequent use of AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, often described as “Google replacements.” However, physicians also highlighted ethical issues and the need for local training and infrastructure improvement. Conclusion: Physicians generally welcome the use of AI in healthcare and research but emphasize the necessity of ethical guidelines, peer collaboration, and formal education. To ensure responsible adoption, addressing infrastructural and trust barriers will be essential for guaranteeing that AI technologies improve rather than undermine patient care and research integrity.
