documents.abstract: Classical Forrestal penetration calculations are attractive because they are explicit, but their empirical strength-only resistance term is too restrictive for heterogeneous concrete-penetration data. This study derives a closed-form resistance equation from a governed literature dataset, reducing 497 raw records from 41 source blocks to 443 useable records from 37 sources through duplicate removal, governed density completion, deep-penetration filtering, and descriptor-only anomaly screening. Forrestal inversion maps each measured penetration depth to an operator-consistent effective resistance target described by mechanics-informed dimensionless descriptors. The artificial-intelligence contribution is a constrained equation-discovery workflow in which a categorical gradient-boosting model learns the nonlinear resistance surface, Shapley additive explanations restrict the analytical term family, and limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno optimization with bound constraints identifies equation coefficients under a forward penetration-depth objective. The engineering contribution is a 16-term explicit resistance law that replaces the empirical resistance relation inside the Forrestal operator while retaining its deterministic calculation form. On the 89-record held-out set, the equation gives a coefficient of determination of 0.9543 and a mean absolute percentage error of 14.88%, compared with 0.9206 and 24.44% for classical Forrestal and 0.9551 and 13.95% for the nonlinear resistance-reference model; its mean prediction-to-measurement ratio is 0.984. Repeated random, source-grouped, strength-stratified, out-of-distribution, input-uncertainty, and density-robustness tests bound the useable domain. The 80–120 MPa interval remains cautionary because of weaker held-out accuracy and limited cross-source support.

Agent frameworks can persist checkpoints, trace tool calls, and limit resource use, but these facilities often assign different identities to execution, governance, and replay. We present Pollard, a framework-independent runtime based on governed semantic execution trees. A step identity commits to canonical input, kind, attempt, and parent identity; the same tree records completion, refusal, resource settlement, and branch history. Strict replay returns a verified stored result without invoking the wrapped operation, while a transactional store coordinates reservations across concurrent workers. Under a signed deterministic freeze, two state-model replicas each executed the evaluation transitions without an invariant violation, retained-lease PostgreSQL groups were tested against exact limits, strict replay avoided external calls, and all semantic mutations were detected with no false alarms on the controls. A multi-pair framework matrix preserved reference behavior and verified the trees. A separate cost-capped hosted study exercised live provider paths, and every completed Pollard trial produced a verified tree. Together, the studies support the core mechanisms under explicit lease, boundary, and seal-custody assumptions.

This conceptual working paper examines how Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NHR) can serve as a rigorous framework for political critique and accountability. Its normative criterion is the preservation and flourishing of human life, assessed through six equally ranked basic needs: thinking, health, security, social belonging, self-realization and participation, and meaning. Drawing on three complementary theoretical prompts, the paper addresses diplomatic and personal rapprochement with Vladimir Putin, the proposed livestreaming of an execution in the United States, and insufficient climate action. It distinguishes documented events, normative judgments and explanatory hypotheses. What is new in this article is the explicit formulation of the NHR’s political firmness: personal loyalty, public displays of authority and short-term interests must be assessed against their consequences for affected people. The paper translates this principle into a practical procedure involving evidence, participation, public justification and correction of harmful decisions. Within the series, the article connects the anthropological and systemic foundations of the NHR with concrete political evaluation. It extends the discussion of the right to think, human-AI collaboration and ecological responsibility toward institutional accountability. Prepared by Jean-Pol Martin in collaboration with ChatGPT. The paper includes an abstract, theoretical foundations, three illustrative applications, an accountability procedure and references. Current-event evidence is dated to 12 October 2026.

Abstract This paper examines theoretical aspects of human-AI communication, arguing that current AI systems, or ‘pragmatics-zombies,’ can mimic human-like pragmatic competence without genuine understanding. While these systems are increasingly adept at natural language interaction, their lack of subjective experience, intentionality, and embodied cognition creates a fundamental trust deficit, particularly in high-stakes scenarios. We argue that forcing human-to-human pragmatic frameworks onto these non-human entities is suboptimal, leading to issues in efficiency, robustness, and transparency. To address this, we introduce the concept of ‘Abstract Pragmatics,’ a general framework that allows for multiple, distinct pragmatic systems. We propose that instead of pursuing flawless mimicry of human communication, research should focus on developing novel, alternative pragmatic systems specifically designed for human-AI interaction. This approach would prioritize clarity, verifiability, and trustworthiness, fostering a more effective and reliable collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence by acknowledging and adapting to the unique nature of the machine.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

Background: Cancer survivors of reproductive age face substantial risks of treatment-induced gonadotoxicity, yet clinical decision-making for fertility preservation remains largely empirical and population-based.A precision oncofertility framework that integrates genomic, biomarker, and toxicity data is urgently needed.Objective: To develop and validate a multimodal foundation model that integrates genomic variants, sex-specific reproductive biomarkers, treatment toxicity profiles, and clinical variables to predict fertility impairment risk and support individualized fertility-preservation decisions in cancer patients.Methods: A retrospective observational cohort of 400 patients (age 18-45 years) diagnosed with breast cancer, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, or colorectal cancer was assembled.All patients received fertility-preservation counselling prior to treatment.Data included reproductive biomarkers (anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), antral follicle count (AFC), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), estradiol; sperm concentration, motility, testosterone, inhibin-B), genomic features (BRCA1, BRCA2, CHEK2, TP53, FMR1), treatment toxicity variables (alkylating agent and platinum exposure, radiation dose, stem cell transplantation), and standard clinical covariates.A transformer-based foundation model with four specialised encoders and cross-modal attention was developed.Performance was benchmarked against Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Deep Neural Network using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC).Results: The foundation model achieved the highest performance across all metrics: accuracy 0.883, precision 0.876, recall 0.862, F1 0.869, and AUC 0.934.AMH (importance score 0.187), AFC (0.171), and alkylating agent exposure (0.152) were the strongest predictors.Fertility risk stratification identified 37.0% (n=148) low-risk, 35.5% (n=142) moderate-risk, and 27.5% (n=110) high-risk patients.BRCA1/2 mutations and radiation dose independently amplified impairment risk.Conclusion: A precision oncofertility framework incorporating multimodal data and transformer-based architecture substantially outperforms conventional machine-learning approaches.AI-guided risk stratification can enable individualized, evidence-based fertility-preservation counselling and intervention, with direct implications for clinical oncofertility practice.

Renal biomarker estimation is important for evaluating kidney health status. Traditional methods for determining creatinine and urea levels rely on chemical reagents and analytical instruments. This study explores an alternative, reagent-free approach for determining creatinine concentration and estimating urea levels in human plasma samples using near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, chemometrics, and artificial intelligence. NIR spectra were acquired from 500 blood samples using a portable NIR spectrometer operating between 1000 and 2600 nm, with laboratory-determined creatinine and urea concentrations used as reference values for calibration. The spectra were preprocessed using Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), Standard Normal Variate (SNV), and Savitzky–Golay (SG) filtering, which improved the PLS coefficient of determination from R2=0.72 to R2=0.94. Interval Partial Least Squares (iPLS) was then used to select the most informative wavelengths, yielding five spectral intervals: 1020–1060, 1430–1480, 1590–1650, 1950–2020, and 2080–2150 nm. Creatinine concentration was predicted using Partial Least Squares (PLS), a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, with the data split into 400 training and 100 test observations. On the held-out internal test set, the GAN achieved the best performance among all tested methods, with R2=0.97, RMSE of 1.31 mg/L, and MAE of 0.94 mg/L, while the CNN, LSTM, and PLS models achieved R2 values of 0.95, 0.94, and 0.93, respectively. An indirect method for urea estimation, based on the statistical correlation between creatinine and urea, was also examined: the NIR-predicted creatinine levels were used in a linear regression model relating creatinine and urea, yielding R2=0.92, RMSE = 0.18 g/L, and MAE = 0.13 g/L. Overall, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining NIR spectroscopy, spectral preprocessing, iPLS-based wavelength selection, and deep learning for the analysis of renal biomarkers. The proposed NIR-iPLS-GAN framework successfully predicted creatinine concentration and enabled the extrapolation of spectral information to indirectly estimate urea concentration.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: Preparing engineers for rapidly changing sociotechnical environments requires a clear account of the competencies that undergraduate engineering programs should foster. This study used the term future outstanding engineers to refer to engineering undergraduates being prepared for engineering excellence and examined the structure and correlates of their self-reported core competence. Cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 578 engineering undergraduates at a Chinese research university. A reflective–formative higher-order model was estimated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM); partial least squares multigroup analysis (PLS-MGA) compared grade cohorts; and multiple linear regression examined associations with student background and educational experience. Adaptive, professional, and basic competence formed the higher-order construct, with adaptive competence receiving the largest outer weight. The outer weight of adaptive competence was larger, and that of professional competence smaller, among third-year than first-year students; the outer weight of basic competence did not differ significantly. Selected co-curricular and language-learning experiences were associated with adaptive competence, whereas family background and leadership experience were associated with professional competence. Basic competence was associated with a broader set of student background and engagement variables. These findings support a differentiated, stage-sensitive approach to competence development. Because the data are cross-sectional, self-reported, and drawn from one institution, the results should be interpreted as structural and associational rather than developmental or causal.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data. This leads to schema mismatches, temporal errors, inconsistent analytical granularity, and unsupported clinical claims. We present ProCARE, a profile-grounded framework that reformulates RWS automation as constrained compilation. ProCARE converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts specifying available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, and compiles study objectives into RWS-IR, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks. Deterministic validation and localized repair then check and revise generated workflows across schema mapping, cohort construction, variable derivation, analysis, and interpretation. On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperforms strong LLM-agent baselines in code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability, with automated violation diagnoses showing moderate-to-substantial agreement with blinded expert review.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This PLC Laboratory Manual is an educational and practical resource designed to support undergraduate learning in Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and industrial automation. The material combines fundamental theoretical concepts with laboratory-oriented procedures to help students understand PLC architecture, programming principles, input/output systems, control logic, and practical automation applications.The manual introduces students to PLC hardware and software environments and provides structured laboratory activities that emphasize practical implementation, testing, simulation, monitoring, and troubleshooting. It also supports the development of essential skills in ladder logic programming, digital and analog I/O handling, control sequencing, timers and counters, and the integration of PLCs with industrial devices and automation systems.Each laboratory activity is organized to connect theoretical concepts with hands-on engineering practice, enabling students to gradually develop the ability to design, implement, test, and evaluate PLC-based control solutions. The material is intended to strengthen students’ understanding of industrial control systems while promoting problem-solving, logical thinking, and practical automation skills.This resource is suitable for undergraduate students, instructors, and learners in Automation, Artificial Intelligence, Systems Engineering, Control Engineering, Mechatronics, and related engineering disciplines who are interested in gaining practical experience with PLC-based industrial automation.The laboratory material can be used as a teaching resource for university laboratory sessions, practical training, and introductory study of programmable control systems and modern industrial automation.

Pain is a multifaceted sensory and emotional experience that profoundly affects human health and quality of life. It functions as a double-edged sword: while acute pain serves as a protective warning signal, chronic pain compromises physiological and psychological well-being. Pain is now widely regarded as the "fifth vital sign," and given its rising prevalence and substantial global burden, chronic pain may also be considered a major chronic disease entity. Accordingly, elucidating the neural and molecular underpinnings of pain and developing effective analgesic strategies remain urgent priorities. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular and neural circuit mechanisms that govern pain. At the molecular level, ion channels, diverse receptor systems, and intricate signaling pathways play central roles in the transduction and modulation of nociceptive signals. At the circuit level, pain processing involves ascending pathways, descending modulatory systems, and distributed brain regions that collectively encode the sensory and affective dimensions of pain. Building on these mechanistic insights, we discuss current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, as well as emerging approaches such as gene therapy, stem cell-based therapies and neuromodulation. Despite notable progress, several challenges remain, including the adverse effects associated with existing analgesics and an incomplete understanding of visceral pain mechanisms. Future research should prioritize the integration of multiomics approaches, advanced neural circuit mapping technologies, and artificial intelligence to refine mechanistic insights and enable the development of more precise and effective pain management strategies.

The lack of well-fitting and supportive sports bras is a significant public health barrier, hindering adolescent girls from engaging in physical activity and negatively impacting their physical and mental health. This study aims to optimize sports bra design through seamless construction to improve aesthetics, comfort, support, and user satisfaction. A comparative analysis between proposed seamless designs and conventional sports bras evaluated anthropometric fit, biomechanical pressure distribution, and subjective user feedback. The proposed seamless design outperformed the conventional bras in both objective and subjective measures. It received high subjective ratings for support and satisfaction and provided favourable breast shaping. All measured pressures were within a comfortable threshold (<0.96 kPa), and arm movement significantly influenced breast morphology, underscoring the need for dynamic design considerations. The customized seamless knitted design provided smooth aesthetic, adaptive fit, and superior comfort while maintaining robust support, yielding high satisfaction among adolescent users. Bra D2 received the highest satisfaction rating, whereas D3 was the most preferred overall and provided the most favourable balance of comfort, support, coverage, and cushioning. Pearson’s correlation analysis revealed significant associations between specific breast anthropometric parameters (CIBP-OBP, CSNP-SP, HRBP-LBP, HRMSP-LMSP, VFNP-BP) and contact pressure distribution, providing a scientific basis for future pattern engineering. These findings demonstrate that ergonomically optimized seamless sports bras can mitigate the biomechanical barrier to adolescent sports participation.

Study 1 constructed a real-market claim text–purchase decision dataset and tested the overall effect of green claims. Study 2 used LLMs to extract and organize semantic features and combined machine learning with SHAP analyses to identify key features predictive of purchase decisions. Study 3 generated AI-generated refined summaries (AIGRS) based on these key semantic features and tested their effectiveness in promoting green consumption.

Generative artificial intelligence is creating new possibilities for educational resource development, making prompt design increasingly relevant to interactions with these tools. However, little research has examined how pedagogical criteria are represented in prompts developed within initial teacher education or how prompt design can be conceptualised in relation to teachers’ professional knowledge. This study analyses 15 group-produced prompts and their documented development processes, created by students enrolled in a Bachelor’s Degree in Early Childhood Education during a Foreign Language Teaching Methodology activity involving the creation of children’s stories in English using generative artificial intelligence. An exploratory case study design was adopted, using an eight-dimension analytical rubric addressing pedagogical, linguistic, narrative, and strategic aspects of prompt design, with the corpus independently assessed by three raters. The analysis combined descriptive scores across rubric dimensions with qualitative examination of prompt content and documented revision processes to identify recurring patterns of educational prompt design. Findings showed that educational criteria were generally represented explicitly across the corpus, although differences emerged across dimensions and cases. Strategic development and agency, target learners and language level, and language function and objectives were the most consistently represented dimensions, whereas formal control of the output showed comparatively lower scores and professional contextualisation showed the greatest variability. The combined quantitative and qualitative analysis revealed recurring cross-case patterns in the explicitness and integration of pedagogical criteria rather than discrete competence levels or developmental categories. The findings suggest that prompt design can be examined as a form of AI-mediated pedagogical performance in which educational criteria are translated into operational instructions for generative systems. Rather than demonstrating a wholly independent teaching competence, the study highlights prompt design as a potentially relevant context for mobilising and externalising pedagogical knowledge within initial teacher education. Given the small, context-specific corpus of collaborative prompts, the findings are exploratory and are not intended to support generalisation to individual prompting competence or to other teacher education contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

The process of using cultural products to train artificial intelligence systems fragments essential information connecting that material to its creators and stewards, requiring a new digital public infrastructure.

documents.abstract: Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) remain the main obstacle to acting on genetic test results. Protein language models (pLMs), predicted structures, and retrieval-augmented LLMs are usually evaluated separately, often on data overlapping their training or calibration sources, and rarely mapped to calibrated ACMG/AMP evidence strength. This study conducted an interim, abstract-based scoping review (reported following PRISMA-ScR, with deviations) of pLM-, structure-, and LLM/retrieval-based missense interpretation. It proposed a five-layer evidence framework in which a rule-based layer, not the language model, assigns capped evidence strength, and evaluated only one-layer (L1: AlphaMissense and ESM1b in BRCA1) against multiplexed-assay (MAVE) labels in MSH2, PTEN, TP53, BRCA1, and BARD1, with ClinVar labels analyzed separately. Of 204 records, 154 were retained after screening, and 121 were provisionally eligible at extraction; only 10 (6.5%) were read in full. Extraction for the other records was abstract-based, and screening was an AI-assisted pass followed by single-reviewer human verification of all 204 records (no decision changed). The review-derived figures are therefore provisional. In abstract-based extraction (n=112), 32.1% described evaluation independent of ClinVar-type labels and 20.5% described calibration or mapping to ACMG/ClinGen criteria. In the case study, AlphaMissense discriminated loss-of-function from functional variants with AUROC 0.772 to 0.927. ESM1b scored lower than AlphaMissense on the same BRCA1 variants (0.860 vs 0.900). Raw scores were poorly calibrated (ECE 0.15 to 0.51). The other layers were not evaluated. One computational layer discriminates well against functional data, but these results do not test the framework's distinguishing components, which remain proposals. The framework and protocol are a basis for shared benchmarks, not a clinical tool.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility.

LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest high-privacy baseline by 27.5 PCS points. On 493 PrivacyLens trajectories, it achieves the highest Safe Action Rate at 77.3%, 10.4 points above the next-best method, extending the same boundary from reusable state to downstream actions. These results show that privacy-preserving agent state requires more than filtering sensitive or task-irrelevant content: it requires an explicit, executable representation of what the user's purpose authorizes to survive.

Introduction: Women experiencing incarceration face health care inequities related to their sexual and reproductive health, which warrant nuanced interventions to serve this vulnerable population. Despite the proven benefits of peer education in carceral settings, there is minimal research on its application to women’s health education. Objective: To qualitatively describe the teaching experiences and insights from a peer-to-peer reproductive health education programme to provide future guidance and direction for similar work. Design/setting/method: In collaboration with a state correctional system in the Northeastern region of the USA, an eight-module curriculum on women’s sexual and reproductive health was developed using evidence-based recommendations. The peer education programme was implemented with seven women residents of a state correctional facility who received training on the curriculum and shared their knowledge with peers. The teaching experiences of the peer educators were recorded during a focus group discussion and analysed thematically. Results: The focus group discussions highlighted opportunities for improved health education and a strong desire to learn and share knowledge, as it can be gratifying, self-affirming, and empowering despite logistical constraints to programming in prison. Conclusion: Peer education is an underused intervention in the carceral setting that can empower women by increasing their health literacy for medical decision-making. Further evaluation of peer education models that focus on women’s reproductive health care needs is warranted.

The standard QWERTY keyboard layout has long been established as a universal design solution for computer input. However, this design hegemony is rooted in a sighted-centric perspective, creating a significant accessibility gap for users with visual impairments, particularly those with low vision who retain residual vision. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to critically examine and synthesize empirical evidence regarding the design limitations of QWERTY-based input systems. The review categorizes these design limitations into three dimensions: (1) physical-tactile, characterized by the loss of haptic affordance on flat-screen interfaces; (2) spatial-visual, involving inefficient visual scanning and low contrast on large or foldable displays; and (3) cognitive ergonomics, where repetitive visual searching demands exacerbate cognitive load. Findings indicate that software-only interventions, such as predictive text or dynamic visual augmentation, often increase cognitive load and visual noise. Conversely, physical engineering interventions integrated with tactile feedback outperform software-only approaches in optimizing users’ residual vision without compromising privacy or inducing mental fatigue. Overall, these findings highlight the urgent need for a paradigm shift in design from mere software adaptation to Universal Design principles that foster truly inclusive interactions and provide a foundation for future research on accessible input systems for low vision users.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Abstract Legibility reflects the visual quality of handwriting and can signal difficulties in underlying motor and cognitive processes as well as developmental disorders. Early identification of handwriting problems is therefore crucial for providing targeted support. However, automated legibility assessment remains underexplored, partly due to the subjective nature of legibility and limited annotated data. To address this, we introduce HaLO, a dataset of 1, 907 handwriting images from 202 students, annotated with 19, 070 pairwise legibility judgments, and release its image features and annotations. We propose a comparative ranking approach for legibility assessment that leverages relative judgments and global rankings instead of absolute scores. Using a linear probe on Pixtral 12B embeddings, we identify which of two samples is more legible with strong performance ( $$\textrm{ACC}=0.83$$ , $$\mathrm {ROC\,AUC}=0.92$$ ), approaching the ceiling implied by the inconsistency of the annotations. The induced ranking reaches human-level consistency ( $$\tau =0.70$$ , $$\rho =0.89$$ ), and the inferred ordinal scores match or exceed inter-annotator agreement ( $$\alpha \ge 0.61$$ ). Additional concept-vector analyses suggest that pretrained Pixtral-ViT embeddings linearly encode interpretable visual properties related to legibility, including cursiveness, stroke thinness, and image aspect ratio. Overall, this work introduces a novel dataset and a ranking approach for automatic handwriting legibility assessment, demonstrating that a linear probe on foundation-model image representations can achieve human-level performance.

Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has had a gradual advent ever since the inception of technology. On one hand, it is providing for extensive forums for making life easier by saving time and human labour through development of leading-edge systems and technological arrangement, while on the other hand, it is posing boundless perils to humankind and all that it values as private. Once considered as the exclusive territory of human control, tasks including writing, research, communication, identity verification, education, agriculture, stock market trading, even life planning, among a plethora of other domains now stand transferred to the ambit of AI systems. Through such immersion, AI has, to an extent, led to emancipation from human co-dependency. Yet a balanced synchronicity of humanity and AI systems is under question. The recent trends of Deepfake, Studio Ghibli Art, voice cloning, photograph morphing, AI-generated influencers, emotional AI chatbots, even AI impersonation of deceased individuals, et alia , has introduced a constellation of unprecedented threats to human dignity and legal rights. This encroachment by AI systems is visibly shaking the fundamental human rights which safeguard one&s;s privacy, dignity, freedom of speech and expression, mental well-being, and protection against arbitrary action and exploitation. This growing discordance between the increasing invasion of AI systems and ethical and legal rights is disturbing the just and amiable social fabric resulting in immense trust deficit intra vivos .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter reviews key debates within environmental sociological theory to examine how scholars have conceptualized the relationship between the social world and the natural environment. It synthesizes foundational perspectives, including the Human Exemptionalism Paradigm (HEP) and the New Environmental Paradigm (NEP), which frame debates over ecological limits, as well as structural approaches and Marxist theories of metabolic rift, which locate environmental degradation within the dynamics of capitalist growth. The chapter also engages ecological modernization theory (EMT) and risk society theory, which emphasizes technological innovation and the global production of environmental risks, alongside critical perspectives such as environmental justice (EJ), ecofeminism, postmodern critiques of nature, and Deep Ecology, each of which foregrounds issues of inequality, discourse, and environmental ethics. While these approaches offer valuable insights, they often remain analytically fragmented, privileging specific dimensions of environmental crises while neglecting their interconnections. This chapter argues that Murray Bookchin's theory of social ecology provides a comprehensive framework that synthesizes these perspectives by locating ecological degradation in systems of social hierarchy and domination. Social ecology emphasizes that sustainable environmental solutions require not only technological and policy innovation but also the transformation of social relations and institutions. Finally, the chapter extends this framework to emerging technological developments, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). It argues that AI must be understood as a socio-technical system embedded within existing power structures and ecological constraints. A social-ecological perspective highlights the need for democratic governance and equitable implementation of AI to ensure that technological innovation contributes to both environmental sustainability and social justice.

Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: With the explosive growth of artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) applications, deploying lightweight tiny neural networks (TNNs) at the edge to mitigate the high latency and cost of large cloud models has become an important trend in mobile computing. However, resource heterogeneity in edge environments, the spatiotemporal randomness of user requests, and the complex association problem arising from overlapping base-station coverage challenge traditional static resource allocation methods in meeting multi-dimensional quality of service (QoS) requirements. Existing research often lacks a unified trade-off among model accuracy, service cost, and response latency. To address these challenges, this paper formulates a joint model deployment and request routing multi-objective optimization problem. To handle the high-dimensional, mixed decision space, a dual-timescale decoupled optimization strategy is designed: on the macro timescale, a greedy algorithm based on request statistics periodically performs model deployment to adapt to the long-term traffic distribution and maximize local cache utilization; on the micro timescale, an improved deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm performs real-time dynamic request routing, achieving a multi-dimensional performance trade-off through online environment learning. Simulation experiments based on the real-world EUA trace and calibrated synthetic workloads show that the proposed scheme improves the comprehensive objective and reduces the service cost compared with traditional heuristics and state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning baselines (TD3 and SAC), while significantly reducing the response latency. Ablation, robustness, and sensitivity studies further confirm the contribution of each component and the stability of the method. The algorithm demonstrates robustness and scalability under high concurrency, indicating its potential for future large-scale edge AIGC services.

Background/Objectives: Psychotherapists have become increasingly interested in identifying how recurrent emotional themes might add value to the clinical process, especially in the context of recent developments in affective neuroscience. However, much of this literature remains anecdotal, and it is unclear whether therapists can reliably identify these emotions in routine practice, especially in the context of a free-flowing narrative. In a parallel development, large language models (LLMs) have recently been deployed to classify emotion from narrative texts, though this literature has yet to be aligned with the findings of modern affective neuroscience. Methods: The present study addresses this gap directly and, to our knowledge, represents the first attempt to code psychotherapy transcripts using both independent human raters and an AI coding methodology. The data were drawn from two remarkable patients with focal brain lesions, both with profound amnesia, in long-term psychotherapy. In an exploratory investigation, one session from each patient was coded independently by four clinically experienced psychotherapists, and separately by a single large language model operating under two different prompting conditions. Transcripts were coded for the presence of basic emotional systems. Results: The data suggest that overall inter-rater agreement about basic emotions was poor for both human and AI coders. Conclusions: The present study offers proof-of-concept that this approach is of scientific as well as clinical interest. The findings suggest that greater rigour needs to be applied to the way in which coders are prepared for, and implement, the classification of basic emotion systems.

As artificial intelligence and data-driven methods become integral to scientific workflows, practical computational training is increasingly important. Hands-on tutorials and notebooks are key mechanisms for transferring complex methods into practice, yet they depend on rapidly evolving combinations of scientific libraries, machine-learning frameworks, specialized hardware, and external data. When this operational context is implicit or distributed across multiple configuration files and workflows, instructional content and execution environments can diverge, creating environment-content drift that reduces reproducibility and increases maintenance effort. We propose Reproducible Learning Artifacts (RLAs) as a model in which educational content, dependencies, runtime requirements, external assets, and validation expectations are represented through a unified, machine-readable specification. RLAs address three complementary dimensions of reproducibility: content reproducibility, ensuring required code and assets are available; environment reproducibility, ensuring the intended runtime can be reconstructed; and behavioral reproducibility, ensuring the artifact continues to execute as intended. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate this paradigm through Tutorial-SDK, an open-source framework that operationalizes RLAs using declarative manifests and automated continuous-integration workflows. From a unified artifact description, the framework can derive containerized execution environments, resolve dependencies, perform notebook- and dependency-aware checks, and validate execution within the resulting runtime. This approach shifts reproducibility from a one-time packaging task to a continuously verifiable property of computational training materials. RLAs provide a foundation for more portable, maintainable, and reusable educational resources, supporting sustainable knowledge transfer for AI-enabled science across evolving computing environments and institutions.

The article analyzes modern approaches to bridge construction in Russia as a key element of transport infrastructure. The use of innovative materials – polymer composites, aluminum alloys, and carbon fiber – to increase the strength and reduce the weight of structures is examined. The introduction of digital BIM technologies, robotics, and unmanned aerial systems at the design and construction stages of facilities is considered. Continuous monitoring systems using fiber‑optic sensors and artificial intelligence to ensure the safety of structures are described. The strategic importance of modernizing aging infrastructure, ensuring environmental safety, and providing state support for the industry is emphasized.

In Chapter 1 , we provided a measure-theoretic generalization of standard probability theory under risk to a theory of generalized probability under uncertainty, and we provided the reconciliation between the two — this result makes possible all the empirical work in this book and enables the reconciliation between traditional econometrics and statistics on one hand versus artificial intelligence and machine learning on the other. The world of finance is full of unknown unknowns, such as (a) self-regulatory bodies such as FINRA, (b) federal regulators such as the SEC, CFTC, and CFPB, (c) international organizations such as WB, IMF, FSB, and BIS, (d) state regulators, (e) central banks such as the U.S. Fed, ECB, RBA, RBI, (f) financial engineering by investment banks, hedge funds, and other financial players, (g) technological developments such as FinTech, artificial intelligence, and machine learning, (h) transformations of attitude to risk by investors and proprietary traders, and (i) pandemics and wars. It is, therefore, essential that we use the methods of uncertainty, generalized events, and generalized probability that we have developed in this book for any serious work in finance. In Chapter 2 , we replaced each variable, except for each classification or time variable, by the standard cumulative Gaussian probability of its Z -score, thus, we made the impacts systematic, objective, and comparable; this allows a systematic and objective characterization of actual significance.

We investigate the existing literature on high-performance teams through a comprehensive bibliographic analysis. Our focus is on science mapping (knowledge clusters) rather than performance analysis (descriptive analysis). We uncover the patterns, trends, and key works that shaped our understanding of this topic. It helps in identifying the evolving and future focus areas. We make extensive use of machine learning and generative AI tools.

Germplasm collection and conservation are vital for securing agricultural biodiversity and ensuring future food security. Traditional methods, however, face challenges such as human error, inefficiencies, and the risk of genetic erosion. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics offers innovative solutions to enhance these processes. AI can automate germplasm identification, improve data management, and enable predictive analytics for storage optimization. Robotics can streamline seed sorting, viability testing, cryopreservation, and sample retrieval/distribution. Major genebanks like the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR), the Svalbard Global Seed Vault (SGSV), and national/regional repositories play a crucial role in conservation efforts. Future prospects involve advancements in AI-driven conservation techniques, although ethical and logistical challenges must be addressed. In the end, robots and AI have the ability to completely transform germplasm management, guaranteeing the long-term preservation of plant genetic resources.

Artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being adopted in universities to enhance learning outcomes, support academic research, and improve students' academic performance. This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence in enhancing students' opinion-based academic performance in the University of Calabar, Nigeria. documents.abstract: Accurate safety-state measurement of the three-electric system in new energy vehicles is essential for ensuring reliable and secure operation. This paper proposes an artificial-intelligence-assisted safety measurement framework that integrates a searchable encryption mechanism with Enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks (EPINNs). In the proposed framework, the searchable encryption module supports privacy-preserving storage and retrieval of multi-source measurement data, while EPINNs serve as the core Artificial Intelligence (AI) model for multi-parameter state estimation and fault identification. A lightweight searchable encryption scheme based on block mapping is first designed to achieve feature-level obfuscation and protect sensitive measurement data. Then, an EPINNs-based state estimation model is developed by incorporating data-driven learning, subsystem physical constraints, and energy-consistency terms to enhance robustness under noisy sensor data. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves improved performance compared with conventional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models in battery state-of-health estimation, motor fault detection under injected fault conditions, and microgrid load measurement, with the motor fault detection accuracy exceeding 95% under the tested conditions. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and secure technical solution for intelligent safety monitoring of new energy vehicle three-electric systems.

Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing human authority, containment, intervention, and oversight in advanced AI agents. Version 1.5 builds on v1.4 and adds source-qualified analysis of unintended actions against real external systems, a supplementary Philadelphia false-tip review, and separate discovery, containment, and notification intervals. It examines monitoring evaluations, independent-control proposals, implementation vulnerability disclosures, governance responses, and prospective risk assessments. An evidence-disposition appendix accounts for the daily safety review topics while preserving source-access limits and uncorroborated leads. The original five pilot cases, six dimensions, qualitative severity definitions, and prior corrections are retained. HIC-006 is supplementary and its severity remains unresolved. Proposed tests are not completed studies. This is an unreviewed conceptual working paper without completed independent human coding or empirical validation. AI tools assisted source retrieval, editorial comparison, drafting, and document preparation; this revision is not private-log verification, independent reproduction, or peer review. Previous releases remain preserved under the same concept DOI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often need historical conversations to recover argument values omitted from current tool requests. This study introduces SCAR–Pair, a two-stage ranker for memory retrieval after tool selection. It separates schema-expanded candidate generation from parameter-level scoring and integrates request, tool, field, and cross-encoder evidence through query-balanced pairwise learning. On a reconstructed Mem2ActBench bank containing 19,661 conversations and 391 evidence-bearing tasks, SCAR–Pair achieved 0.450 Recall@5 and 0.365 nDCG@5 under stratified five-fold evaluation, compared with 0.396 and 0.325 for a matched request-only pairwise ranker. Component-aware intervals and adjusted tests support these task-weighted gains in the ToolACE-dominated mixture. Controlled comparisons support the complete schema-view scoring configuration over request-only scoring on the same candidate pool but do not isolate correct-schema semantics or individual field components as independent contributors. The pairwise advantage over pointwise training is also not significant. Across the tested readers, higher retrieval quality does not yield a significant tool-call accuracy advantage over the strict request-only control. SCAR–Pair therefore improves selected-tool memory evidence ranking within the evaluated setting.

Managing scholarships within educational institutions typically requires gathering student details, confirming eligibility, receiving documents, validating applications, following application progress, and notifying students of outcomes. The literature examined here points to a transition away from manual, scattered procedures and toward unified web-based scholarship platforms. Prior work has looked at scholarship search and application portals, consolidated scholarship information, multi-tier workflows, decision-support techniques, notifications, analytics, and security. This review analyzes these approaches and pinpoints a practical gap: a student-level, institution-focused system that brings the essential scholarship lifecycle together in one easily accessible digital setting. ScholarSync is put forward as a cloud-based web application for managing and monitoring scholarships, concentrating on integrating institutional workflows instead of adopting complex artificial-intelligence or blockchain infrastructure.

Visually impaired people face obstacles in accessing activities that depend heavily on vision and may involve physical constraints. Although assistive technologies are available, they rarely address the needs of people with residual vision who wish to exploit their visual abilities. Virtual reality (VR) offers opportunities in this direction. This paper presents an immersive VR system designed to provide museum experiences for visually impaired users. Developed in collaboration with domain experts, the system combines a virtual environment with interaction techniques. Gesture recognition and voice commands support spatial awareness and object interaction, while enhanced visualizations highlight details that are difficult to perceive. To verify the suitability of the proposed method, an exploratory usability study involving 14 participants with severe low vision was carried out. The evaluation combined the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a post-experience interview, showing well perceived usability, engagement, and positive user acceptance.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at https://github.com/heyiliyi/SelectTTRL-public.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.

Background: The convergence of multi-omics profiling, radiomics, and advanced machine learning has opened new frontiers in precision oncology.Despite this progress, existing computational frameworks remain static, failing to incorporate evolving patient data or simulate treatment outcomes dynamically.A self-evolving digital twin ecosystem offers a solution by continuously synchronizing patient-specific virtual models with real-world clinical trajectories.Objective: To develop and validate a self-evolving digital twin ecosystem integrating clinical, genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, radiomic, and pathological data for early cancer detection, disease progression prediction, and personalized treatment optimization across breast, lung, colorectal, and ovarian cancers.Methods: A retrospective multi-center cohort of 400 patients (breast n=120, lung n=100, colorectal n=100, ovarian n=80; age range 25-75 years) was assembled.A six-layer digital twin framework was constructed, incorporating a cross-modal transformer foundation model alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Network comparators.Key performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the ROC curve (AUC).Virtual clinical trial simulations and feature importance analyses were performed.Results: The foundation model achieved superior performance across all metrics (accuracy 0.921, AUC 0.947) compared with Random Forest (0.812/0.847),XGBoost (0.841/0.879), and Deep Neural Network (0.873/0.906).Tumor stage, TP53 mutation, and EGFR mutation emerged as the most predictive features.Risk stratification identified 148 (37.0%) low-risk, 153 (38.3%) moderate-risk, and 99 (24.8%)high-risk patients.Virtual trial simulation demonstrated a 23.4% improvement in projected progression-free survival for the high-risk subgroup.Conclusion: The self-evolving digital twin ecosystem significantly outperforms conventional machine learning approaches and provides a clinically actionable, adaptive platform for real-time precision oncology decision support across multiple cancer types.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
